source_text: Quid igitur hinc conficiatur, adverte; non adhaerere negationem gratiae laudi humanae naturae, quin immo haec quattuor ita esse coniuncta, ut alterum sine altero teneri nequeat, sed infamia naturae pariat negationem gratiae et laus gratiae pariat praedicationem naturae; ista enim in quamvis sibi partem reciprocari possunt. Bene ergo dixisti: Natura humana, si malum esset, salvanda non esset [n246] ; hoc enim dicunt utrumque Manichaei, malam videlicet carnis naturam nec posse salvari per gratiam nec debere.
pass_a_gloss: What therefore is accomplished from here, advert; that the negation of grace does not cling to the praise of human nature, nay rather these four are so conjoined that one cannot be held without the other, but the infamy of nature begets the negation of grace and the praise of grace begets the preaching of nature; for these can be reciprocated into whichever part. You have said well therefore: Human nature, if it were evil, would not be to be saved; for the Manichaeans say both, namely an evil nature of flesh and that it can neither be saved through grace nor ought.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Observe the conclusion: denying grace does not attach to praising human nature. Rather, these four positions are so connected that one cannot be maintained without the other: defaming nature produces denial of grace, and praising grace produces commendation of nature. These implications can run in either direction. You therefore spoke well: ‘If human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). The Manichaeans say both things: flesh’s nature is evil, and it neither can nor ought to be saved through grace.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
